analysis.one_liner: Raises statutory damages for copyright infringement and directs harsher sentencing guidelines for digital piracy.
analysis.headline: Congress passed the bill without a single recorded vote in two days, and the President signed it on December 9, 1999, raising maximum copyright damages per work from $20,000 to $30,000.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill raises the damages a court can award a copyright owner without proof of actual loss: the minimum per work goes from $500 to $750, the maximum from $20,000 to $30,000, and the maximum for willful infringement from $100,000 to $150,000. It also directs the U.S. Sentencing Commission to quickly write guidelines implementing the criminal penalties in the No Electronic Theft (NET) Act. Notably, it applies to any lawsuit filed after enactment, even for infringement that happened earlier. It cleared the House without objection and the Senate by unanimous consent, and became Public Law 106-160.
analysis.who_benefits: Copyright owners — record labels, movie studios, publishers, and other rights holders — gain far larger potential awards per infringed work without having to show actual financial loss, and prosecutors get guidelines to seek heavier sentences for digital piracy.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Record labels, studios, and rights holders

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum statutory damages per infringed work from $500 to $750 and the maximum from $20,000 to $30,000, sums a court can award without proof of actual loss [S2] [S3].
Raises the maximum additional damages for willful infringement from $100,000 to $150,000 [S2] [S3].
Directs the Sentencing Commission to promulgate emergency guideline amendments within 120 days to implement the criminal sentencing mandate in the No Electronic Theft (NET) Act [S2] [S3].
Makes the higher damages apply to any suit filed after enactment, regardless of when the infringement occurred, so claims over older conduct can carry the new penalties [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Anyone accused of copyright infringement, including ordinary individuals: a single copied song or file can now trigger an award of at least $750 per work with no proof of harm, and the sums bear little relation to actual damage. Defendants and courts bear the cost of litigation over older conduct that the bill makes retroactively subject to higher awards.

drawbacks.text: The new statutory damages apply to any lawsuit filed after enactment even for infringement that occurred before the law passed, exposing people to higher penalties for past conduct [S3].

A minimum award of $750 per work vastly exceeds the actual loss from casual infringement by an individual — a copied track that costs 99 cents can carry a four-figure judgment — and the bill added no exception for ordinary consumers [S3].
The bill directed harsher criminal sentencing guidelines for intellectual property crimes under the NET Act, extending the reach of criminal penalties for file sharing and digital copying [S2] [S3].

The bill passed both chambers within two days by unanimous consent with no recorded debate or amendments, so no member had to vote on the record and no public hearing is reflected in the action history [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A credible argument exists that higher penalties deter large-scale commercial piracy, which does protect the creators and companies whose work is sold. But the bill's design gives rights holders awards many multiples of any real harm from individual copying, applies the new penalties retroactively to suits over past conduct, and produced no countervailing protections for consumers or fair-use users. The costs fall on ordinary people exposed to enormous liability; the benefits accrue almost entirely to the copyright industries.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced on November 18, 1999, it passed the House without objection that same day and the Senate by unanimous consent the next day, and the President signed it on December 9, 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Howard Coble introduced H.R. 3456 on November 18, 1999; the House Judiciary Committee was discharged at his request the same day, and the House passed it without objection with no roll-call vote [S5].
The Senate passed it the next day, November 19, 1999, without amendment by unanimous consent — again with no recorded vote [S5].
The bill had no cosponsors listed [S4].
The President signed it on December 9, 1999, and it became Public Law 106-160 [S5] [S3].
The final text applies the higher damages to any action brought on or after enactment regardless of when the alleged infringement occurred [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Copyright owners — record labels, movie studios, and other rights holders — gained substantially larger statutory awards and heavier sentencing guidelines, while no opposing interest was recorded in either chamber's action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Record labels, studios, and rights holders

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were taken in either chamber — the House passed it without objection and the Senate by unanimous consent — so no party split is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Music and movie industries (record labels, studios)
industries.note: The bill multiplies the damages they can collect per infringed work — up to $30,000, or $150,000 for willful infringement — without proving actual loss, and applies the higher awards to suits over past conduct. Those sums can dwarf any real harm from individual copying, and the industries' gain is exactly the liability ordinary users face.

industries.industry: Copyright litigation industry (plaintiffs' counsel and enforcement firms)
industries.note: Larger statutory ranges per work make infringement claims far more valuable to pursue and settle, since the penalty no longer needs to match actual harm. The people on the other side of those suits are overwhelmingly individuals.
As copyright holders, they share in the higher damages available for infringement claims. The benefit comes at the expense of anyone sued for copying.
